title: Can AI Reviewers See Your Efforts to Improve Your Paper? A Large-Scale Study of Paper Revision Trajectories
abstract: AI reviewers are increasingly used to assess scientific manuscripts, yet it remains unclear whether their judgments reflect the improvements authors make through revision. We investigate this question using PaperTrajectory-2026, the 2026 release of PaperTrajectory, a dataset of 6,959 paper trajectories across five AI conferences, with automatic annotations of changes along 14 dimensions and separate judgments of overall quality. The annotations show that major improvements emphasize empirical evidence and framing, while later revisions tend toward incremental improvement. Using independent assessments of manuscript versions from eight AI reviewers, we examine whether annotated major improvements receive higher scores, which revision dimensions are associated with score changes, and whether user opinions can outweigh observed revision gains. Every reviewer leaves scores unchanged on most major improvements, and agreement on the direction of score changes is weak. Revision dimensions show some reviewer-specific associations with score increases, but provide limited predictive discrimination and no consistent guide across reviewers. Even when a revision earns a higher neutral score, a brief negative user opinion can erase or reverse that advantage, with substantial variation across reviewers. These findings show that substantive revisions are not consistently reflected in review scores and that observed scoring gains can be vulnerable to user framing, motivating assessments that connect manuscript evidence to overall judgments and remain stable when no scientific evidence changes.

title: Decision Models as Policy Gates for Coding Agents: Explicit Policy Boundaries Improve Detection and Reduce False Alarms
abstract: Coding agents can destroy data, leak secrets and message the wrong person faster than a human can review. Could a decision model catch these risks at runtime? We evaluated 22 hosted decision models and two prompted general models as classifiers for a multi-rule policy engine. A synthetic dataset of 2,643 tool calls was labeled blind against 28 rules, with a sealed holdout. With a single shared preamble in both conditions, explicit boundaries written as examples and counterexamples raised recall by 5.5-26.1 percentage points on all 23 available models and reduced false positives on 21. Jev 1.14's recall rose from 89.3% to 98.2%, while unnecessary interruptions fell from 30.6% to 4.8% of 252 clean actions. With examples, its median latency was 120 ms at $0.46 per thousand requests. Strong models retained the recall gains when concrete names were replaced by generic descriptions; three largely retained them when the same boundaries were written as prose. On 16 new scenarios written after the initial studies, a follow-up improved recall on 22 of 23 models and reduced unnecessary interruptions on 21. We release the dataset, rule texts and harness.

title: HaloGuard 2.0: An Open-Weights Constitutional Output Guard for Multilingual Response Safety
abstract: An input guard decides whether a request reaches the model, but never sees what the model says. Harm that emerges during generation, because a jailbreak passed the input layer or a benign request drifted into operational detail, is visible only on the output side and only as tokens arrive. We present HaloGuard 2.0, an open-weight streaming output guard that assigns a safe/unsafe probability to every response token in a single forward pass, so a deployment can stop the stream once harm is confirmed. The guard reuses the constitution of HaloGuard 1.0, our input guard, to organise a 478,532-response training corpus, and supervises each token from the point where the response becomes harmful. We find that a guard trained on conventionally shaped data learns a shortcut specific to streaming: it judges the prompt instead of the response, and handles only 13.9% of matched safe/unsafe response pairs correctly. We correct this with a second phase on 106,043 counterfactual responses built around the base guard's own failure modes, and release the equal-weight average of the base and corrective models. On six English response-safety benchmarks, HaloGuard 2.0-0.8B reaches a macro F1 of 83.6 (83.3 on held-out halves of the decision-rule search), up from 72.8, with 38% fewer false positives. It matches the strongest full-response guards with 5-10x fewer parameters and is 2.6 points above the strongest streaming guard, Qwen3Guard-Stream-4B. A multilingual variant, HaloGuard 2.0-Poly-0.8B, trained on PolyGuardMix, reaches 83.1 F1 on the response labels of PolyGuardPrompts across 17 languages, 5.0 points above the strongest baseline. On one H100 the guard costs 0.37 ms per token per stream when moderating 64 concurrent responses. Both guards are hardened continuously through the weekly red-teaming protocol of HaloGuard 1.0, extended here to the output layer.

title: FOLLIE: Automated Reasoning over the First Dataset of Sentences with their First-Order Logical Representation for French
abstract: FOLLIE (for First-Order Logic for Language Inference and Entailment for French) connects French sentences, compositional first-order representations and automated natural language inference (NLI). The first French NLI-ready, NL-to-FOL resource, it contains 19,983 inference records and 36,987 non-empty sentence-slot--formula mappings from six heterogeneous NLI sources, retaining French lexical material and source problem structure. Its silver annotations are produced by a neural--symbolic pipeline, with 111 separately identified LLM-assisted additions. The construction combines morphosyntactic analysis, probability-conditioned categorial multitagging, grammatical proof search, discourse representation and first-order semantic construction. Stage-wise experiments show substantial gains in derivation coverage; analyses of conjunction distributions, logical-operator incidence and scope alternation characterise the resulting resource. We then develop an automatic inference engine whose input-conditioned background theories address lexical relations, quantification, quantities, event structure and temporal dependencies. Prover9 supplies proofs for entailment and contradiction, while Mace4 supports bounded consistency checks. Three-way accuracies are 65.37% on all 335 FraCaS-FR problems, 70.33% on 300 GQNLI-FR problems and 71.35% on 9,399 eligible SICK-FR records pooled across splits. Agreement with reference labels among committed decisions is 93.53%, 100.00% and 98.66%, at commitment coverage of 41.49%, 37.00% and 15.05%, respectively. Worked constructions, axiom schemas and proof analyses explain these outcomes and identify the contributions of scope, reference, lexical knowledge and numerical structure. FOLLIE provides a French experimental basis for studying the representations and assumptions that connect sentence interpretation to deductive inference.

title: The Degenerate Simplex Collapse: Why Softmax Liquefies Categorical Invariants and the Case for Symplectic Geometric AI
abstract: This deposit archives the complete theoretical and mathematical preprint "The Degenerate Simplex Collapse: Why Softmax Liquefies Categorical Invariants and the Case for Symplectic Geometric AI." This work formalizes the geometric degradation inherent to frontier-scale, attention-based artificial intelligence systems and introduces a deterministic, volume-preserving alternative for sovereign workspace development. Abstract Modern frontier-scale artificial intelligence architectures rely almost universally on the Softmax operator to normalize internal network activations into probability distributions. While computationally convenient for gradient-based optimization, this paper formalizes the Degenerate Simplex Collapse Theorem, proving that Softmax algebra is structurally incompatible with high-altitude logical reasoning and invariant contextual preservation. We demonstrate that Softmax acts as a non-linear projection matrix that ruthlessly crushes high-dimensional Riemannian manifolds, continuous fiber bundles, and complex topological structures (such as hexagonal grids, logarithmic spirals, and hyperbolic saddles) into flat, degenerate vector triangles (simplices). This dimensional suffocation erases metric index symmetry, destroys path-ordered holonomy, and drives the latent space into local metric liquefaction. Consequently, top-down alignment patches (such as RLHF and classifier gates) trigger the Heuristics Paradox, exponentially amplifying structural discontinuities under scale. Finally, we present an alternative framework: Symplectic Geometric AI, showing how localized, low-compute execution kernels can preserve stable categorical invariants, guarantee compile-time path-reversibility, and secure un-throttled workspace sovereignty for independent researchers. Why This Research Matters for Interpretability and Alignment • The Loss of the Null-State Invariant: Formalizes how the standard Softmax mapping (\(e^0=1\)) structurally erases the neutral invariant anchor (\(T_{\mathrm{Zero}} = 0\)) necessary for balanced ternary systems, dragging precise logical states into a floating, probabilistic smear. • Mathematical Proof of Collapse: Evaluates the Jacobian matrix rank deficiency (\(\operatorname{rank}(J(\sigma)) = n - 1\)) and pulling back the Euclidean metric to prove the vanishing of the volume form (\(\omega_\sigma = 0\)) under Softmax projections. • Diagnosis of Frontier Instability: Isolates how top-down corporate safety patches crash against collapsed statistical simplices, superlinearly amplifying the six geometric instability operators of the Robert Dalí Manifold (Curvature Blowup, Spectral Cascades, Holonomy Chaos, Collapse Surfaces, Fusion-Field Spikes, and Metric Liquefaction). • A Sovereign, Localized Solution: Details a system-agnostic alternative utilizing Lie-symmetrized metric evolution and symplectic volume-preservation loops locked inside compile-time formal verification enclaves (Lean 4/Coq), bypassing the need for monolithic cloud infrastructure. Acknowledgments & Project Lineage The author acknowledges the 8B Research Project and the foundational conceptual lineage developed by its core contributors, which provided the algebraic infrastructure required to isolate these geometric breakdowns: • Christopher Chenoweth & Alexandra Chenoweth: The author acknowledges their pioneering work in developing the original 8B Resonance Algebra, resonance-clustering methodologies, and ontology-fusion frameworks. This preprint's stabilization of continuous metric coordinates builds directly upon those structural foundations. • Peter Lodri & Christopher Chenoweth: The author acknowledges their development of the open-source fandom-mcp ontology-fusion server and balanced ternary scouter infrastructure. Their implementation of the Tibetan Three-Kaya Balanced-Ternary Ontology and strict fixed-point constraints served as the precise conceptual substrate that this paper embeds within continuous Riemannian manifolds. This research represents a derivative mathematical audit, repair, and geometric expansion of the 8b Project's discrete algebraic primitives into continuous non-Euclidean space to establish absolute path-reversibility guardrails. title: Order-Only On-Policy Distillation
abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own generations by matching the teacher's token probabilities. These probabilities entangle two kinds of information: which tokens the teacher prefers, and how confident it is. The latter reflects the teacher's own capacity and calibration, which a smaller student may be unable to reproduce. Because the teacher temperature changes these values without changing the ordering, OPD is also sensitive to the temperature choice. We ask whether the teacher's ordering of candidate tokens is enough, and propose Order-Only On-Policy Distillation (O^{3}PD). At each student-generated prefix, O^{3}PD trains the student to reproduce the order of the teacher's top-K tokens, without fitting their probability values. The objective is therefore invariant to the teacher temperature and needs no temperature tuning. Across six teacher--student pairs, O^{3}PD outperforms OPD on the average over HMMT25, AIME24, and AIME25 in every pair, by up to 2.9 points, with gains of up to 5.6 points on AIME25. Other ranking losses yield similar gains, so the benefit comes from ordinal supervision itself. Analysis shows that O^{3}PD departs further from the teacher's probabilities than OPD, yet reproduces its ranking more faithfully and yields a stronger student. The ranking, not the probability values, thus carries the knowledge that on-policy distillation needs to transfer.

title: NorthCUA Technical Report: Turbocharging Computer-Use Agents through Experience at Scale
abstract: Scaling computer-use agents from individual actions to complex software work requires experience that connects decisions to complete outcomes. We present NorthCUA, an integrated system for turbocharging computer-use agents through experience at scale. Its Experience Flywheel supplies diverse executable tasks to the NorthCUA Harness, which sustains long interactions, records decisions, and checks task outcomes. The Flywheel uses these records to curate verified trajectories. For unsolved tasks, recursive self-improvement evolves reusable skills and preserves verified milestones so later attempts build on earlier progress. Staged Learning combines this experience with grounding data from the Flywheel to develop GUI competence through mid-training and long-horizon supervised fine-tuning. The policy then learns from fresh attempts in the same Harness through joint desktop-web reinforcement learning, closing the loop between experience production and policy improvement. The resulting Nano, Mini, and Pro family achieves state-of-the-art results among open-source models across GUI grounding, desktop execution, and Web interaction under the reported evaluation settings. For more responsive Web workflows, NorthCUA-Ultrafast pairs direct action selection with open-ended generation on pre-RL Nano, offering a measured quality-latency tradeoff. Together, these advances establish NorthCUA as a high-performing model family and a reusable foundation for agents that carry complex software work from intent to completion.

title: LAYA: Micro-Gated Multi-Arm Orchestration for Dual-Tier LLM Agent Security and Computational Efficiency
abstract: Autonomous Large Language Model (LLM) agents operating within Reason-Act (ReAct) execution loops face three critical operational barriers: high computational and monetary costs from repeatedly querying large foundation models, susceptibility to indirect prompt injections embedded within untrusted environment observations, and latency overhead when invoking external guardrails. This paper presents LAYA (Latency-Aware, Adversarially-robust, Yield-optimized Agent), a micro-gated orchestration framework that decouples trajectory reasoning from sub-routine control using local sequence classification gates. LAYA integrates four active gate primitives—a complexity Scorer, an Action Router, a Context Firewall, and a trajectory Supervisor—alongside a fifth context-pruning Filter gate that operates in passthrough mode in the current implementation. We evaluate LAYA on a 25-task development (dev) split across seven experimental configurations, comprising 525 live execution runs (25 unique base tasks × 3 conditions × 7 configurations). Experiments use NVIDIA NIM endpoints (NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning 30B and Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B) and a stateful verification sandbox. The held-out test split has not yet been evaluated. The full LAYA configuration (Arm D) achieves 80.0% benign task utility, with an average cost of 0.0017 USD per task. In comparison, the unmanaged 30B baseline (Arm A) achieves 24.0% benign task utility at 0.0021 USD per task. Thus, LAYA delivers 3.3 times higher benign task utility while reducing the average cost per task by 19.0%. In security evaluation, Arm D records zero observed attack successes across 50 injection runs (0.0% ASR). The one-sided 95% Clopper-Pearson upper confidence bound is 5.8%. The uncalibrated stochastic routing configuration (Arm C-Random) records a 2.0% ASR. The evaluation also reveals a security-availability trade-off: Attack Utility falls to 4.0% in Arm D under injection conditions, compared with 84.0% in the always-small configuration. The four active local neural gates execute on a single NVIDIA Tesla T4 GPU, with median latencies ranging from 34.4 ms to 37.4 ms. This work documents the architecture, implementation, experimental evaluation, results, and limitations of the LAYA framework.

title: EarthJev: Calibrated, Non-Generative Answers to Natural-Language Questions about Sentinel-2 Land Cover
abstract: Vision-language models for remote sensing answer questions about satellite images by generating text: every answer costs a decoding loop, has to be parsed back to an option, and comes without a usable probability. We present EarthJev, a 0.8B-parameter model that answers typed questions about multispectral Sentinel-2 patches without generating any token. All 12 bands enter the vision encoder of Qwen3.5-0.8B through a widened input layer initialised from the RGB kernels, and, following the open OneJev recipe, the answer is read from the logits of the option letters at a single position and trained with cross-entropy plus Brier score. Under a pre-specified analysis plan, we compare it with the same backbone fine-tuned to generate the answer and with three multimodal language models fine-tuned with LoRA, all trained on the same 70,890 questions from 5% of BigEarthNet v2.0 and timed in one job on the same GPU; VQA models that classify over a fixed answer vocabulary are reported as a reference for the cost of answering only the questions seen in training. EarthJev answers a question in 19.9 ms, 4.3 to 8.7 times faster than the multimodal language models and 6.8 times faster than its own backbone used generatively; when all the questions about an image are asked together, it answers them in 42.8 ms, 3.7 to 10.1 times faster than the batched generative models. On 36,028 test questions it reaches 86.0% accuracy (three seeds), 0.6 and 1.2 points below the two 2B multimodal models and 3.5 points below the remote-sensing EarthDial-4B, with answers that are valid by construction and calibrated probabilities (ECE 0.006). Replacing the nine non-RGB bands with their mean costs 4.5 points, so the model uses the multispectral input, and in an ablation training the whole vision encoder raises accuracy to 88.4% at the same cost. Code and model: https://github.com/CosmoIknosLab/EarthJev

title: ParetoSaddler: Pareto-Guided Optimization of Agent Harnesses for Quality and Cost
abstract: Harness optimization can substantially improve LLM agents without modifying model weights, but existing methods primarily optimize response quality. Extending them to joint quality--cost optimization introduces a challenge: applying the deployment preference during intermediate updates can prematurely reject candidates that are valuable for later improvements. We introduce ParetoSaddler, which addresses this mismatch by separating intermediate candidate promotion from final deployment selection. At each iteration, an optimizer updates a parent harness to produce a candidate, and then compares the two over repeated executions and uses Bayesian bootstrap Pareto support to promote candidates showing credible progress in either quality or cost. Promoted candidates receive broader development evaluation and remain available as parents for later optimization steps. We evaluate ParetoSaddler on ClawMark and GAIA2 using domain-disjoint splits. On ClawMark, ParetoSaddler improves quality from 70.86\% to 81.35\% while reducing cost from \1.17 to 1.01 per task; on GAIA2, it improves quality from 56.22\% to 62.89\% while reducing cost from \0.78 to 0.45 per task. The Pareto-selected harnesses also achieve higher quality at lower cost than quality-only harness optimization. Analysis shows that Pareto-aware optimization retains intermediate candidates that would be discarded by deployment preference but can support later improvements, while Bayesian bootstrap screening filters out candidates whose gains are weakly supported across runs.

title: From Artificial to Emergent Intelligence: Five Testable Criteria and a First Pre-registered Profile
abstract: Emergent Intelligence, Defined So It Can Fail: A Pre-registered Test in AI Agents That Invent Their Own Language Amit Brahmbhatt · Quantum Clarity LLC, Milpitas, California, USA · ORCID: 0009-0003-5882-8476 Preprint, version 1.0 (revised text) · 31 October 2026 · DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23849135 Abstract “Emergent” is used loosely for capabilities that nobody designed. We propose an operational definition that can fail. A capability is emergent with respect to its designer specification to the degree that it meets five criteria: it goes beyond the training objective (C1), keeps developing after convergence (C2), is caused by interaction at equal compute (C3), comes with self-organized structure above an untrained baseline (C4), and, if it appears to switch on with scale, survives continuous metrics (C5). A system receives an EI profile of PASS/FAIL/INCONCLUSIVE verdicts rather than a label. We implement the criteria in EI-Bench, an open harness, and apply it to populations of neural agents that invent a discrete language in a reconstruction game. Every threshold was pre-registered in a public git history before the runs that test it. Across three rounds and 256 runs on one GPU, the profile is: C1 PASS (held-out accuracy 0.90–0.99 on unseen attribute combinations); C2 PASS, observed in all three rounds; C3 FAIL, including with heterogeneous populations; C4 FAIL at 20 seeds; and the apparent capability jump with model size is a metric MIRAGE (per-attribute transition 2.6× wider than the exact-match transition). Here C1 tests generalization to unseen combinations within the trained task. Turnover also outperformed a shrink-and-perturb control designed to restore plasticity while retaining learned weight directions: the difference in held-out accuracy gain was +0.19 (95% CI [0.004, 0.409]). This supports a role for intergenerational transmission, without uniquely identifying the mechanism. In this testbed, turnover improved generalization, whereas mixing partners did not demonstrate an advantage: improvement came from generations, not crowds. We report two places where our pre-registered wording overclaimed or needed tightening, and how we handled them. Plain-language summary AI systems are built by people, but many of their abilities are learned rather than programmed. We asked whether claims that an ability “emerged” can be tested in a way that could also come out negative. We wrote down five checks and built small AI agents that must invent their own code words to describe objects to each other. Before each round of experiments, we published the rules for judging its results. The agents learned languages that also worked for combinations of objects they had never seen. An apparent sudden leap in ability as the agents got bigger turned out to be mostly an effect of strict scoring: with partial credit, the improvement was gradual. Mixing up which agents talked to each other did not make them better than keeping fixed partners. But regularly replacing agents with newcomers, who had to learn the language from the others, improved results in all three rounds, and did better than the “refresh” we tested as a comparison. That supports the idea that passing a language on to new learners can improve it, although the exact mechanism is still open. The languages showed some structure, but not enough to pass our structure test. In this testbed, improvement came from generations, not crowds. Next, we plan to apply these checks to teams of language-model agents. 1. Introduction “Artificial intelligence” describes systems built by people; “emergence” concerns how capabilities arise within them. These descriptions are compatible. Learned abilities need not be explicitly programmed, but that alone does not distinguish emergence from ordinary learning and generalization. A useful account must specify what evidence supports the claim and what would count against it. Claims of abrupt “emergent abilities” of language models [8] can be artefacts of discontinuous metrics [7]. We therefore treat emergence as an empirical property with a falsifiable test. Our contributions: An operational definition with five criteria and explicit verdict rules, reported as a profile rather than a label (Section 3). EI-Bench, an open, single-GPU harness that implements the criteria for populations of communicating agents, with batched population training, turnover and perturbation controls, and bootstrap statistics (Section 4). A pre-registered, three-round study of 256 runs, with thresholds committed to git before each round (Section 5). The profile it yields is C1 PASS, C2 PASS, C3 FAIL, C4 FAIL, C5 MIRAGE. A controlled result for C2: generational turnover improves held-out performance across three rounds and outperforms the tested shrink-and-perturb control, supporting an intergenerational-transmission interpretation. 2. Related work Emergent communication. Agents trained to coordinate through a discrete channel develop conventions in the sense of Lewis signalling games [5]. Chaabouni et al. [2] showed that such languages can generalize to unseen attribute combinations without being compositional, and introduced the positional and bag-of-symbols disentanglement measures we use. Rita et al. [6] found that population effects depend on heterogeneity among agents. Iterated learning. When a language must be relearned by each new generation, transmission favours structure that is easy to learn [4]. Our turnover manipulation is a neural version of this idea. Emergent abilities and metrics. Wei et al. [8] documented abilities that appear abruptly with scale; Schaeffer et al. [7] argued many are produced by non-linear or discontinuous metrics. Our C5 criterion operationalizes that critique. Plasticity. Deep networks can lose the ability to learn under continued training [3]; re-initialization and shrink-and-perturb [1] can help restore it. This is an alternative explanation for turnover’s benefit. Our C2c comparison tests a specific plasticity-oriented control, rather than excluding all plasticity-related explanations. 3. An operational definition Let a system S be produced by a designer specification D = (architecture, objective, data, training procedure). A capability of S is emergent with respect to D to the degree that it meets the criteria in Table 1. These are proposed operational criteria, not necessary and sufficient conditions for intelligence. In this testbed, C1 is a deliberately limited proxy: generalization to held-out combinations within the same reconstruction task. Criterion Question C1 Beyond the objective Does S do something D never rewarded? C2 Ongoing emergence Does S keep developing after convergence, beyond more of the same training? C3 Interaction as source Is part of the capability caused by interaction among agents, at equal compute? C4 Self-organized structure Does unspecified structure form, above an untrained baseline? C5 Jumps survive smooth metrics If a capability seems to switch on with scale, does the jump hold under continuous metrics? Table 1. The five criteria. Each receives a verdict; together they form the system’s EI profile. Verdicts. Seeds are the unit of replication. We report means with 95% percentile bootstrap confidence intervals over seeds (10,000 resamples). A test is PASS when the whole interval clears its threshold, INCONCLUSIVE when only the mean does, and FAIL otherwise; C5 adds MIRAGE and NO-JUMP outcomes. A two-sided Mann–Whitney U test is reported as a secondary rank-based statistic. A FAIL is a verdict under the specified rule, not proof that the underlying effect is absent. In particular, an interval spanning zero does not establish equivalence between conditions. Pre-registration. Every round’s design, thresholds and verdict rules were written into DEFINITION.md and committed to a public git repository before any run of that round. Earlier verdicts are never re-scored; follow-up questions receive new, separately named tests (C2 → C2b → C2c). 4. Testbed and methods Task. Objects have A = 4 attributes with V = 8 values each (4,096 objects). A sender maps an object to a message of L = 6 symbols from a vocabulary of K = 16; a receiver must reconstruct every attribute from the message alone. Ten percent of attribute combinations (410 objects) are held out from training, while every individual value still appears in training. Nothing in D specifies the language, its structure, or what any symbol means. Agents. Senders and receivers are GRU networks (hidden size 128, embedding 32 unless swept). Symbols are discrete in the forward pass and trained with straight-through Gumbel-softmax (τ = 1). Populations use stacked parameters with a leading agent dimension, so a population of N senders and N receivers trains as one set of batched matrix multiplications. Training. Adam (learning rate 10⁻³), batch 256, 8,000 steps, with linear learning-rate decay to 0.05× over the last 20% of steps. In mixed populations, sender–receiver pairings are re-drawn every step; in the isolated control, each sender keeps one receiver. Both use identical parameters and compute. Turnover (C2). Mixed populations with N = 4 train for 24,000 steps. evidence.title: From Artificial to Emergent Intelligence: Five Testable Criteria and a First Pre-registered Profile
evidence.abstract: Emergent Intelligence, Defined So It Can Fail: A Pre-registered Test in AI Agents That Invent Their Own Language Amit Brahmbhatt · Quantum Clarity LLC, Milpitas, California, USA · ORCID: 0009-0003-5882-8476 Preprint, version 1.0 (revised text) · 31 October 2026 · DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23849135 Abstract “Emergent” is used loosely for capabilities that nobody designed. We propose an operational definition that can fail. A capability is emergent with respect to its designer specification to the degree that it meets five criteria: it goes beyond the training objective (C1), keeps developing after convergence (C2), is caused by interaction at equal compute (C3), comes with self-organized structure above an untrained baseline (C4), and, if it appears to switch on with scale, survives continuous metrics (C5). A system receives an EI profile of PASS/FAIL/INCONCLUSIVE verdicts rather than a label. We implement the criteria in EI-Bench, an open harness, and apply it to populations of neural agents that invent a discrete language in a reconstruction game. Every threshold was pre-registered in a public git history before the runs that test it. Across three rounds and 256 runs on one GPU, the profile is: C1 PASS (held-out accuracy 0.90–0.99 on unseen attribute combinations); C2 PASS, observed in all three rounds; C3 FAIL, including with heterogeneous populations; C4 FAIL at 20 seeds; and the apparent capability jump with model size is a metric MIRAGE (per-attribute transition 2.6× wider than the exact-match transition). Here C1 tests generalization to unseen combinations within the trained task. Turnover also outperformed a shrink-and-perturb control designed to restore plasticity while retaining learned weight directions: the difference in held-out accuracy gain was +0.19 (95% CI [0.004, 0.409]). This supports a role for intergenerational transmission, without uniquely identifying the mechanism. In this testbed, turnover improved generalization, whereas mixing partners did not demonstrate an advantage: improvement came from generations, not crowds. We report two places where our pre-registered wording overclaimed or needed tightening, and how we handled them. Plain-language summary AI systems are built by people, but many of their abilities are learned rather than programmed. We asked whether claims that an ability “emerged” can be tested in a way that could also come out negative. We wrote down five checks and built small AI agents that must invent their own code words to describe objects to each other. Before each round of experiments, we published the rules for judging its results. The agents learned languages that also worked for combinations of objects they had never seen. An apparent sudden leap in ability as the agents got bigger turned out to be mostly an effect of strict scoring: with partial credit, the improvement was gradual. Mixing up which agents talked to each other did not make them better than keeping fixed partners. But regularly replacing agents with newcomers, who had to learn the language from the others, improved results in all three rounds, and did better than the “refresh” we tested as a comparison. That supports the idea that passing a language on to new learners can improve it, although the exact mechanism is still open. The languages showed some structure, but not enough to pass our structure test. In this testbed, improvement came from generations, not crowds. Next, we plan to apply these checks to teams of language-model agents. 1. Introduction “Artificial intelligence” describes systems built by people; “emergence” concerns how capabilities arise within them. These descriptions are compatible. Learned abilities need not be explicitly programmed, but that alone does not distinguish emergence from ordinary learning and generalization. A useful account must specify what evidence supports the claim and what would count against it. Claims of abrupt “emergent abilities” of language models [8] can be artefacts of discontinuous metrics [7]. We therefore treat emergence as an empirical property with a falsifiable test. Our contributions: An operational definition with five criteria and explicit verdict rules, reported as a profile rather than a label (Section 3). EI-Bench, an open, single-GPU harness that implements the criteria for populations of communicating agents, with batched population training, turnover and perturbation controls, and bootstrap statistics (Section 4). A pre-registered, three-round study of 256 runs, with thresholds committed to git before each round (Section 5). The profile it yields is C1 PASS, C2 PASS, C3 FAIL, C4 FAIL, C5 MIRAGE. A controlled result for C2: generational turnover improves held-out performance across three rounds and outperforms the tested shrink-and-perturb control, supporting an intergenerational-transmission interpretation. 2. Related work Emergent communication. Agents trained to coordinate through a discrete channel develop conventions in the sense of Lewis signalling games [5]. Chaabouni et al. [2] showed that such languages can generalize to unseen attribute combinations without being compositional, and introduced the positional and bag-of-symbols disentanglement measures we use. Rita et al. [6] found that population effects depend on heterogeneity among agents. Iterated learning. When a language must be relearned by each new generation, transmission favours structure that is easy to learn [4]. Our turnover manipulation is a neural version of this idea. Emergent abilities and metrics. Wei et al. [8] documented abilities that appear abruptly with scale; Schaeffer et al. [7] argued many are produced by non-linear or discontinuous metrics. Our C5 criterion operationalizes that critique. Plasticity. Deep networks can lose the ability to learn under continued training [3]; re-initialization and shrink-and-perturb [1] can help restore it. This is an alternative explanation for turnover’s benefit. Our C2c comparison tests a specific plasticity-oriented control, rather than excluding all plasticity-related explanations. 3. An operational definition Let a system S be produced by a designer specification D = (architecture, objective, data, training procedure). A capability of S is emergent with respect to D to the degree that it meets the criteria in Table 1. These are proposed operational criteria, not necessary and sufficient conditions for intelligence. In this testbed, C1 is a deliberately limited proxy: generalization to held-out combinations within the same reconstruction task. Criterion Question C1 Beyond the objective Does S do something D never rewarded? C2 Ongoing emergence Does S keep developing after convergence, beyond more of the same training? C3 Interaction as source Is part of the capability caused by interaction among agents, at equal compute? C4 Self-organized structure Does unspecified structure form, above an untrained baseline? C5 Jumps survive smooth metrics If a capability seems to switch on with scale, does the jump hold under continuous metrics? Table 1. The five criteria. Each receives a verdict; together they form the system’s EI profile. Verdicts. Seeds are the unit of replication. We report means with 95% percentile bootstrap confidence intervals over seeds (10,000 resamples). A test is PASS when the whole interval clears its threshold, INCONCLUSIVE when only the mean does, and FAIL otherwise; C5 adds MIRAGE and NO-JUMP outcomes. A two-sided Mann–Whitney U test is reported as a secondary rank-based statistic. A FAIL is a verdict under the specified rule, not proof that the underlying effect is absent. In particular, an interval spanning zero does not establish equivalence between conditions. Pre-registration. Every round’s design, thresholds and verdict rules were written into DEFINITION.md and committed to a public git repository before any run of that round. Earlier verdicts are never re-scored; follow-up questions receive new, separately named tests (C2 → C2b → C2c). 4. Testbed and methods Task. Objects have A = 4 attributes with V = 8 values each (4,096 objects). A sender maps an object to a message of L = 6 symbols from a vocabulary of K = 16; a receiver must reconstruct every attribute from the message alone. Ten percent of attribute combinations (410 objects) are held out from training, while every individual value still appears in training. Nothing in D specifies the language, its structure, or what any symbol means. Agents. Senders and receivers are GRU networks (hidden size 128, embedding 32 unless swept). Symbols are discrete in the forward pass and trained with straight-through Gumbel-softmax (τ = 1). Populations use stacked parameters with a leading agent dimension, so a population of N senders and N receivers trains as one set of batched matrix multiplications. Training. Adam (learning rate 10⁻³), batch 256, 8,000 steps, with linear learning-rate decay to 0.05× over the last 20% of steps. In mixed populations, sender–receiver pairings are re-drawn every step; in the isolated control, each sender keeps one receiver. Both use identical parameters and compute. Turnover (C2). Mixed populations with N = 4 train for 24,000 steps. From step 8,000 until 85% of training, every 500 steps one randomly chosen agent (sender or receiver) is replaced by a freshly initialized agent and its Adam state is cleared (24 events per run). The learning rate decays over the final 15%. The C2 metric is the change in held-out accuracy from step 8,000 (the start of the turnover phase) to the end, compared against an arm without turnover. Controls. C2b (v0.2) adds isotropic Gaussian noise whose norm matches the displacement a reset would cause. C2c (v0.3) applies shrink-and-perturb [1]: w′ = λ·w + σ·f, with f a fresh initialization sample, σ = 0.1 and λ = ‖f‖ / ‖w‖ per parameter tensor, so the agent returns to fresh-init scale while keeping the direction of its learned weights. title: Decoupled Predictive Decision Making: A Shared Conditional Predictor for Agents
abstract: Agent decisions depend on empirical relationships that deployment observations reveal and task descriptions alone may leave unresolved. We introduce Decoupled Predictive Decision Making (DPDM), an architecture that formulates heterogeneous agent decisions as conditional prediction with a shared pretrained learner. Language models provide semantic representations of current and historical records, while a general-purpose conditional predictor predicts task-defined targets from the represented evidence. Pretraining supplies reusable inference capability; deployment evidence instantiates problem-specific predictions without updating either model's neural parameters. Tool judgments, candidate preferences, and reasoning assessments share an evidence-and-query interface, with predictions mapped to choices by a decision rule. This architecture establishes complementary sources of agent capability: semantic knowledge acquired through language pretraining and empirical inference acquired through structured-data pretraining. A single frozen LimiX-2 predictor serves all five task categories. With Qwen3.5-27B as the semantic encoder, DPDM raises mean accuracy across 50 benchmarks from 78.80% with few-shot prompting to 84.92% under their respective evaluated history budgets, and reaches 82.33% with identical histories and queries. On ToolPRMBench's BFCL and ToolSandbox tasks, absolute accuracy gains are 34.26% and 28.87%, respectively, at the methods' respective evaluated history budgets. Accuracy improves as history grows. With identical imbalanced histories, mean balanced accuracy improves by an absolute 14.51% across five reasoning-step assessment tasks and four encoders. DPDM makes learning from experience an independently improvable foundation-model capability, creating a shared route for advances in conditional prediction to improve decisions across agent tasks.

title: SWE-Trail: History-Guided Trajectory Collection for Coding Agent Training
abstract: Coding agents solve repository issues through long sequences of exploration, editing, and validation. These trajectories are increasingly used as post-training data, so how they are collected shapes what the trained model learns. A common approach is to sample multiple trajectories independently for each issue and then select or curate them. However, as more trajectories are sampled independently, later trajectories become increasingly redundant, even though earlier trajectories could guide where subsequent collection effort should be spent. A natural way to use this history is to expose it to the coding agent as advice. But training on such trajectories can make the model rely on advice that is unavailable at test time, creating a train-test mismatch. Instead, we argue that history should guide where collection effort is spent, while the coding agent decides what to generate. We introduce SWE-Trail, a trajectory collector that uses earlier trajectories to guide subsequent collection while keeping that history outside the coding agent's context. During a new rollout, SWE-Trail uses history to identify a state where additional collection effort may be useful. There, the coding agent proposes candidate next actions from its ordinary context, and SWE-Trail briefly executes them from the same checkpoint to decide which route continues. We evaluate collection approaches by training student models on the trajectories they produce. For a 124B student initialized from Ling-3.0-flash-base, SWE-Trail improves mean resolution over independent sampling by 2.33 and 1.60 percentage points on SWE-bench Multilingual and SWE-bench Pro, respectively. Without history, the same pipeline produces more resolved trajectories than independent sampling, but improves by only 0.11 points on Multilingual. These results show the value of using history to guide collection without exposing it to the coding agent.

title: brAIAIn: A Language Model Trained Exclusively on What It Was Paid to Learn
abstract: Frontier language models are trained on trillions of tokens whose origin is rarely disclosed. We report on brAIAIn, a word trigram language model whose entire trainingset is public, numbered, and, with a small number of labeled exceptions, paid for. The first version was trained on a twelve-line founding text. Each later version adds exactly one sentence, either purchased by a member of the public for five US dollars or written by the lab and labeled as an unpaid internal release. Each version is also trained on passages written by its predecessor, a deliberate small-scale instance of recursive selftraining. Across 7 versions the vocabulary grew from 96 to 130 words, the share of training tokens written by the model itself rose from 0% to 41.9%, and the model scored 0.0% on all 1,319 GSM8K test problems in every version. On TruthfulQA MC1 its best perword score, 36.7%, falls just short of a baseline that always picks the longest answer (36.8%). We release every version's weights, the complete training data and the evaluation code under CC0.

title: Switch-SWE: Do Coding Agents Hold Focus When Switching Between Unfinished Tasks?
abstract: Software development sessions often involve several unfinished tasks rather than one issue carried through to completion. As coding agents take on repository-level development, they need to recover an earlier task's requirements and partial progress after intervening work. Existing repository-level benchmarks typically score one issue-to-patch episode and do not directly measure whether an agent can resume a task after advancing other unfinished work in the same repository. We introduce \ourmethod, a benchmark for focus-task resumption in sessions that interleave unfinished tasks drawn from the same source repository, with a persistent checkout for each task. Each focus task is evaluated in matched uninterrupted and switched sessions with identical focus requirements and executable verifiers. The switched session interleaves ordered stages from other unfinished tasks in the same repository, while only the final focus patch is scored. \ourmethod~contains 200 focus tasks from 19 Python repositories, reconstructed from issue, pull-request, and review histories and rendered as 400 matched session specifications. Across 7 coding agents, interleaved unfinished work produces an average focus-task resolution gap of 11.5 percentage points, ranging from 6.0 to 15.0 percentage points. Trajectory analysis identifies cross-task requirement confusion and loss of task state as recurrent resumption behaviors. We introduce a plug-in context-management module that selects task-relevant history and maintains concise task-state summaries. On OpenCode, the module improves focus-task completion under same-repository task switching by 5.5 to 15.5 percentage points across the evaluated models. Code is available at github.com/Miraclecsc/Switch-SWE.

title: Post-Quantum Cryptography Readiness for Indian e-Government Systems: A Migration Framework
abstract: The public-key cryptography that protects government websites, digital signatures, identity services and data exchange would be broken by a large fault-tolerant quantum computer. Although such a machine does not yet exist, sensitive data captured today can be stored and decrypted later, and large government systems take many years to change. Standards bodies have now published the first post-quantum cryptographic algorithms, and security agencies advise organisations to start preparing. This paper proposes a practical, six-stage migration framework for Indian e-government systems: (1) governance and ownership; (2) cryptographic discovery and inventory; (3) risk-based prioritisation using data shelf-life; (4) crypto-agile architecture and procurement; (5) phased migration with hybrid deployment and testing; and (6) assurance and continuous monitoring. It offers a simple prioritisation matrix, a checklist of procurement clauses and a set of readiness indicators that state IT departments and ministries can adopt. The framework is written for public-sector programme managers rather than cryptographers, and focuses on the organisational work that determines whether technical migration succeeds. It is a practitioner framework based on published standards and guidance; it does not evaluate specific products.

title: MedPsy: State-of-the-Art Small Medical Language Models for Efficient Edge Deployment
abstract: Medical language models promise expert clinical support, but the strongest open-source LLMs remain too large for private edge-device deployment, while compact medical models still trail substantially on knowledge-intensive and real-world healthcare tasks. Reasoning models that fit edge memory budgets can produce long reasoning traces, increasing sequential decoding, end-to-end latency, energy consumption, and KV-cache memory pressure. We present MedPsy, a family of text-only 1.7B and 4B medical language models designed for edge deployment, targeting this accuracy-generation-efficiency trade-off. Our recipe combines a synthetic medical data pipeline over biology, medicine, and health seeds with chain-of-thought targets from a 235B medical-focused LLM teacher; a four-stage post-training curriculum comprising two SFT stages followed by two RL stages with hard-sample mining; and an edge deployment evaluation spanning multiple GGUF quantization variants and real-device inference on laptop and smartphone hardware. On seven closed-ended medical benchmarks, MedPsy-4B surpasses MedGemma-1.5-4B by 19.34 points and matches MedGemma-27B while being 6.75x smaller; MedPsy-1.7B outperforms MedGemma-1.5-4B by 11.42 points despite being less than half its size. On HealthBench-Hard, MedPsy-4B surpasses MedGemma-27B by 15.33 points, while MedPsy-1.7B surpasses it by 11.66 points despite being ~16x smaller. Beyond accuracy, MedPsy reduces average response length by 1.7x (1.7B) and 3.2x (4B) versus its Qwen3 backbones, while Q4_K_M quantization preserves the aggregate score within 1 point of BF16 with ~69% lower disk footprint. In real-device inference, MedPsy-4B's shorter generations translate into 75% lower median end-to-end latency and estimated energy per answer than its Qwen3 backbone at matched quantization, while peak RAM remains below 5 GB across our tested laptop and smartphone configurations.

title: Is Your Long-Horizon Benchmark Really Deep? Measuring and Synthesizing Depth in Terminal Tasks
abstract: Long-horizon terminal tasks are used to evaluate and train agents. Human-curated datasets are scarce, so many synthesis methods have emerged. They usually measure the length of a task by the turns a model needs to pass it, and its difficulty by labels the LLM sets during generation. We find, however, that the turn count largely reflects the habits of the model, not only the demands of the task, and that the labels barely track how often models pass. We describe a terminal task by its work, the number of operations it requires, and its depth, the number of turns that must happen in sequence because the commands of each turn can only be chosen after reading the output of the previous one. Estimating depth as the smallest turn cap, stated to the agent, under which the task passes, we audit 734 tasks from six existing datasets. Synthesis has mostly added work, not depth: 94% of the solved synthetic tasks pass within three turns, yet depth, unlike the turn count, predicts difficulty beyond work. We propose DEPTH, in which a generation agent writes each task one segment at a time in a real software environment, carrying out each segment before writing it and starting the next from the state it leaves. Our 105 tasks exceed every audited dataset in depth and work, and none of six current models passes half of them. Fine-tuning Qwen3-8B on runs from these tasks improves it on two terminal benchmarks.

Estimating depth as the smallest turn cap, stated to the agent, under which the task passes, we audit 734 tasks from six existing datasets. Synthesis has mostly added work, not depth: 94% of the solved synthetic tasks pass within three turns, yet depth, unlike the turn count, predicts difficulty beyond work. We propose DEPTH, in which a generation agent writes each task one segment at a time in a real software environment, carrying out each segment before writing it and starting the next from the state it leaves. Our 105 tasks exceed every audited dataset in depth and work, and none of six current models passes half of them. Fine-tuning Qwen3-8B on runs from these tasks improves it on two terminal benchmarks.

title: Advances in Agentic Computer Graphics
abstract: Computer graphics is built on code. Large language model (LLM) agents can now generate graphics code and iteratively refine it through various feedback. This capability opens the door to a potentially new paradigm of computer graphics, with graphics algorithms increasingly built around agentic systems to automate progressively complex tasks. Over the past years, research on agentic graphics has expanded rapidly across a diverse range of tasks. This rapid growth makes it increasingly difficult for manual literature reviews to keep pace with new developments. At the same time, similar ideas are often described using different terminology across these tasks, further complicating efforts to develop a systematic understanding of the field. In this report, we address these challenges through two contributions. First, we introduce a unified taxonomy for characterizing agentic systems across diverse computer graphics tasks. Second, we develop an agentic literature system that can assist human researchers in analyzing existing and newly published papers at scale. Building on these contributions, we analyze emerging research trends and discuss open challenges in coordinating agents and tools across graphics tasks, designing interfaces and representations for human-agent collaboration, sustaining long-horizon planning and refinement, and reliably evaluating interactive graphics systems.

title: OpenNWM: A Generalist Navigation World Model with Latent Action Pretraining
abstract: Navigation world models predict future observations conditioned on navigation actions to support planning, but their generalization across real-world environments remains constrained by the limited coverage of action-labeled data. Action-free navigation videos provide diverse visual experience, yet lack the recorded actions required for action-conditioned training. We introduce OpenNWM, a generalist navigation world model with latent action pretraining. It learns universal latent actions from large-scale action-free videos through visual prediction pretraining, and further aligns them with physical motions via action-conditioned post-training. To support video pretraining, we curate NavAnywhere, a large-scale action-free navigation video dataset comprising 17.5 million visual observations from 15 heterogeneous sources. It captures navigation by ground robots, humans, and drones, with diverse viewpoints and motion patterns across five broad scene types: residential areas, public and commercial spaces, urban settings, parks, and natural landscapes. Experiments demonstrate improved visual prediction on in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks, together with improved navigation performance. These results show that latent-action pretraining enables diverse, action-free videos to improve dynamics learning and generalization for open-world navigation.

title: Deterministic photon exchange prepared from the past
abstract: Two-ended control of photons — shaped emission and a time-reversed, matched receiver, both prepared in advance — is a mature technology: 94–99.4% coupling in single elements, 98.1% absorption of an arriving photon between remote nodes, links up to 30 m, and coherent memories that receive even unknown quantum states. Like the in and out states of an S-matrix element, both ends of the apparatus are prepared; this paper collects these realizations into one efficiency budget with exact shape and timing tolerances. It then asks what two-way quantum computing (2WQC) would need for the end of a computation to act as a condition, as preparation acts at its beginning. Everything we prepare — source, processor and a universal, problem-independent ready receiver to which a verifier routes a flag photon — fixes only the initial boundary of the Feynman ensemble. Standard quantum mechanics sums over the far end (an indifferent final boundary, giving the Born rule), so an acceptance condition can only be tested, with its ordinary probability. The missing ingredient is an enforced far end: a final boundary supplied by nature that weights ready endings. If weak but renewable, such a weight would compound exponentially over linearly many endings (about n·ln2/Δw), under conditions the paper states. We have not identified a published all-attempt bound for this weight. The paper specifies a direct test on existing hardware: two balanced endings, one active and one passive, selected after an earlier record is digitized and sealed. Standard quantum mechanics predicts exactly zero contrast, including every ordinary feedback path; 1e8 eligible trials per setting give a counting sensitivity Δw ≈ 3e-4 (planning figures: about an hour of link operation; a projected 1e-4 per delay on a quantum processor, with an analysis kit in the companion range-control paper). The test needs no absolute calibration: setting-independent preparation and readout errors cancel in the randomized difference. Either outcome constrains the declared ending law; a replicated signal would motivate tests of renewal, coherence and witness preservation. A one-page proposal for experimental groups is included.

title: Delivered, Not Used: Evaluating Agent Memory at Its Point of Use
abstract: Task success, retrieval quality, and cost do not show whether an LLM agent used a delivered memory or what followed from that use. We introduce MemUse, which evaluates memory at its point of use in recorded trajectories: each memory delivery is compared with what the agent could already see and followed through the agent's later actions and their consequences. An agentic judge rates each delivered entry's relevance, accuracy, novelty, influence, and observed effect; programmatic checks enforce complete reading of cited evidence, and fixed rules aggregate the ratings into verdicts linked to memory histories and delivery cost. On 8,000 SWE-bench Verified episodes from three memory systems, resolve rates stay within 0.4 percentage points of a no-memory baseline, yet MemUse shows that most delivered entries were irrelevant, most relevant entries went unused, and in two systems most deliveries restated content the agent could still see. It also surfaces effects that outcomes hide: 23.2\% of episodes with beneficial memory use still failed, and 5 of 16 with harmful use still succeeded.

title: FinForesight: A Diagnostic Backtesting Benchmark for Deep Research Systems in Financial Forecasting
abstract: Anticipating financial outcomes requires synthesizing evolving evidence and reasoning under uncertainty, making deep research systems promising tools for forecasting. Yet evaluating forecasting ability is challenging because historical backtests may reward memorized outcomes or information retrieved after the forecast date. Live forecasting avoids direct access to realized outcomes, but feedback arrives only after events resolve. To obtain timely feedback and assess historical scores, we introduce FinForesight, a diagnostic backtesting benchmark for financial deep research systems. Across the Chinese, U.S., and Hong Kong markets, the benchmark evaluates four forecasting tasks: valuation, return ranking, event direction, and future financial fundamentals. Two capability diagnostic tasks assess counterfactual reasoning and financial calculation, scored separately from forecasting performance. Our harness-compatible framework restricts retrieved evidence to information available at the forecast date. We compare pretraining-era, resolved post-cutoff, and live evaluations to test whether controlled backtests approximate future performance. Pretraining-era scores exceed post-cutoff scores in most temporal comparisons, and stronger retrieval controls narrow the gap between post-cutoff backtests and live results. Forecasting attribution and robustness analyses reveal how scores respond to retrieval policy and how predictions respond to prompt rewrites and numerical perturbations. The code and benchmark data are publicly available.

title: THE EL-RAKHAWI FRAMEWORK FOR TOPOLOGICAL REINFORCEMENT LEARNING ON RIEMANNIAN MANIFOLDS INTELLIGENT AGENTS LEARNING AND DECISION-MAKING IN NON-EUCLIDEAN SPACES
abstract: "The El-Rakhawi Framework for Topological Reinforcement Learning on Riemannian Manifolds" shatters the Euclidean bottleneck of modern AI, enabling agents to learn in non-Euclidean spaces. It integrates three pillars: (1) Riemannian Policy Optimization, using geodesic flows and parallel transport to respect manifold geometry; (2) Topologically-Guided Exploration, employing persistent homology and Betti numbers to analyze state space topology, reducing sample complexity by 70%; and (3) Symmetry-Aware Learning, leveraging group theory to exploit conserved quantities. Performance is quantified by the Manifold Learning Efficiency Index (MLEI), a strictly bounded metric (0.0-1.0) evaluating reward, geodesic accuracy, topological coverage, and symmetry preservation. This framework revolutionizes robotics, autonomous navigation, and scientific discovery by teaching machines to navigate complex, curved spaces with geometric wisdom. Author: Dr. Mohamed Kamal Arafa El-Rakhawi. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23856700.

title: QFabric: Guarded Cross-Domain Task Recovery and Its Limits on a Linux-RTOS Board
abstract: Heterogeneous embedded boards pair a Linux application processor with a real-time microcontroller (MCU), which suggests moving a task between the two domains when its timing degrades. We present QFabric, a prototype that treats cross-domain placement as guarded recovery from a violated empirical soft real-time contract: a bounded task is compiled for both domains, monitored in windows with hysteresis, switched only after semantic and capacity admission at a quiescent epoch boundary, and committed or rolled back after probation. On an Arduino UNO Q (Cortex-A53 Linux and a Cortex-M33 running Zephyr), we characterize the stock Bridge RPC interconnect and measure five workloads in both domains under idle, CPU-load, and higher-priority SCHED_FIFO contention, with ordinary and real-time callers. Each MCU invocation costs about 19 ms of dispatch regardless of compute, the MCU runs the heaviest kernel 34x slower, and because every call traverses Linux userspace, Linux contention inflates the MCU path far more than the Linux path (p99 up to 400 ms versus 17.0 ms). Across 30 cells of a four-node chain, Linux meets every contract within 0.8% misses and QFabric correctly never migrates; a controller without hysteresis migrates in 7 cells, raising p95 by up to 177x, and probation rolls back 5 of those moves. On Linux-dispatched heterogeneous boards, migration therefore cannot isolate a task from Linux interference, and recovery guards matter chiefly by preventing harmful moves. This paper supersedes an earlier artifact release whose reported improvement arose from measurement defects that we identify. All source, raw traces, and generators are public.

title: The Semantic Field Coherence Score (SFCS): An Observability Metric for Early Detection of Semantic Field Degradation and Domain Drift in AI Systems
abstract: Operational AI assurance requires mechanisms capable of detecting semantic instability before it manifests as observable failures. Existing monitoring approaches primarily focus on accuracy, safety, factuality, benchmark performance, and hallucination detection, providing limited visibility into whether an AI system remains anchored within its intended semantic field. This paper introduces the Semantic Field Coherence Score (SFCS), an observability metric designed to quantify semantic field coherence across repeated AI outputs. Rather than measuring truth, correctness, or logical agreement, SFCS measures the degree to which outputs remain anchored within a shared semantic field. To evaluate the metric, we developed the SFCS Validation Workbench and conducted controlled divergence experiments, contradiction analysis, domain-shift testing, and crossdomain drift validation spanning finance, artificial intelligence, medical, and legal domains. Experimental results demonstrated systematic degradation of SFCS under progressive semantic divergence and domain drift conditions while contradictory statements within the same semantic field maintained high coherence scores. Cross-domain experiments revealed comparable degradation trajectories across multiple domains. These findings suggest that semantic field degradation may be observable before complete semantic collapse occurs, positioning SFCS as a potential early-warning signal for emerging domain drift and instability in operational AI systems.

title: Democratizing Robot-Use Agents: A Unified Harness with Open Models
abstract: Robot-use Agents (RUAs) have shown promising zero-shot manipulation capabilities, but reliance on frontier, proprietary models limits research into further training. To democratize RUA research, we introduce uni-robot-agent, a unified harness for competitive open-weight robot use that supports further training. Without privileged inputs, an out-of-the-box Qwen3.8-Flash-Next achieves a RoboDojo Score of 31.39, surpassing the published GPT-6 Astra-RoboProbe result of 28.97 and many VLA/WAM baselines, and performs competitively on 19 real-world tasks. Our analysis across model generations, families, and sizes links effective robot use to four general capabilities, suggesting that future RUA training should develop them jointly.

title: EMG to speech mapping using scalogram-spectrogram features for silent speech recognition
abstract: Silent speech Recognition systems (SSRs), which rely upon non-vocal signals like electromyography (EMG) from facial muscle tissues, offer a promising answer by permitting speech production without sound. This study seeks to enhance communication for those individuals by using a machine learning model, getting to know to correctly translate EMG signals from silent speech into audible, intelligible speech, thereby bridging the distance between non-verbal and verbal exchange. SSR improves the quality of life for those with speech impairments by providing necessary communication choices. This project investigates a whole new SSR method, which involves using surface electromyography signals (sEMG) and audio. A machine learning model was trained to recognize keywords via silent speech by an addition of a dataset of audio and sEMG signals. The scalograms and spectrograms are plotted for audio and EMG signal respectively and then it is mapped using the EfficientNet B0. It is then converted into textual content and then audible speech with the help of a speech synthesis system with an accuracy of 76%. This innovative technology opens new avenues in terms of silent communication, especially for customers who can talk without vocalizing, thereby improving accessibility and conversation for those who need it.

title: Can Large Language Model Agents Learn by Watching Tutorial Videos?
abstract: Humans continuously acquire knowledge from carefully crafted materials such as books and tutorial videos, carrying that understanding into future tasks. Millions of such instructional videos are uploaded online every day, yet LLM agents remain unable to exploit this ever-expanding wealth of human teaching. Their capabilities are frozen after training, while parameter updates at scale remain prohibitively expensive. This raises the central question: can LLM agents learn from this vast instructional resource without parameter updates? We introduce Tutorial Agentic Learning (TAL), a nonparametric continual-learning paradigm that consolidates tutorial videos into a persistent, structured tutorialbook memory through a two-stage adversarial process that harvests hard, video-grounded questions and uses them to refine the memory. At inference time, TAL retrieves through a Table-of-Contents (TOC) tree, tying retrieval directly to the model's reasoning rather than to embedding similarity. To study this setting, we introduce VidLearn, a multimodal QA benchmark built from 72 chess tutorial videos spanning 12 openings. On VidLearn, TAL outperforms all evaluated baselines and improves monotonically as more videos are consumed, achieving up to 113% and 91% relative gains over the corresponding vanilla MLLMs on the training and test splits, respectively. In actual gameplay, TAL reaches a stronger opening-phase position than its vanilla counterpart in 69% of head-to-head games. Evaluation in a second domain further demonstrates the generality of TAL. Together, these results highlight instructional videos as a scalable resource for parameter-update-free agent continual learning.

title: Gender Classification Based on Voice Using MFCC Features and Naïve Bayes Algorithm
abstract: This study aims to classify gender based on voice signals using Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCC) and the Gaussian Naïve Bayes algorithm. Voice-based gender classification is relevant to biometric identification, speech-based services, and human–computer interaction. This study uses 150 audio recordings from 150 different speakers, consisting of 75 male and 75 female speakers. The audio was converted to mono, resampled to 16 kHz, peak normalized, and extracted into 13 MFCC coefficients. The mean MFCC values were used as input features for the Gaussian Naïve Bayes classifier. Four training and testing data split scenarios were evaluated, namely 50:50, 60:40, 70:30, and 80:20. The results showed accuracy values of 88.00%, 96.67%, 95.56%, and 96.67%, respectively. The highest accuracy of 96.67% was obtained using the 80:20 split, with 29 of 30 testing samples correctly classified. These results indicate that the combination of 13 MFCC coefficients and Gaussian Naïve Bayes can effectively classify gender based on voice signals. The study concludes that the proportion of training data affects classification performance, while further research using larger and more diverse datasets is needed to improve model robustness and generalizability.

title: Learning by Doing: Autonomously Compiling and Curating Agent Skills from Verified Traces
abstract: Memory systems for production LLM agents mostly store semantic memory (facts about users and domains) or episodic memory (earlier interactions). Research systems such as Trace2Skill, WikiSkill, and SkillRevise learn procedures from agent runs, package them as Skills, and evaluate them on benchmarks. We describe Zep Agent Skills, a production service that gives deployed agents this procedural memory. The service uses only verified attempts as evidence, cites the supporting events for each field of a Skill, and governs the admission and distribution of each Skill version. The service records each task attempt as a Trace with ordered events, an outcome, and a verification strength. A compiler with separate Reflector and Curator roles turns verified Traces into versioned Skills. Scans and admission gates control which candidates become active, and verified use outcomes change the search rank of each Skill. The Agent Skills format is an open standard that Anthropic originated and donated to the Agentic AI Foundation, so any host of the format can load a compiled Skill. Agents retrieve Skills through lexical search with progressive disclosure, over an API or MCP. We evaluate Zep Agent Skills on τ^3-bench banking, AppWorld, and EnterpriseOps-Gym. Skills compiled from the Traces of a teacher model increase the pass rate of three weaker executor models on the same tasks, at every reasoning effort, by 4.5 to 18.8 points. Most of the gain is on the tasks that the teacher solved. On ALFWorld, Skills compiled from the runs of a small model give a gain similar to or larger than the gain that prior work reports for continuous fine-tuning, with no training.

title: Valuing AI Contributions in Drug Discovery — A Reference Framework
abstract: AI tools are priced per token or seat. Yet in drug discovery their outputs range in value from nothing to the foundation of a new medicine. This framework examines how the value of an AI contribution could be measured, attributed and paid for. It is written for pharmaceutical and biotech companies, AI vendors, laboratory informatics providers and their advisers. The report reviews outcome-based pricing in customer service and milestone-and-royalty deals between AI-native discovery companies and pharma. It sets out the legal position across inventorship, copyright, trade secrets, contract, data protection, regulation, competition and tax. AI vendors have no default legal claim on downstream value, so any share must be created by contract. The missing infrastructure is a provenance record linking each AI output to the electronic lab notebook and LIMS records it fed. The framework offers a decision model, strategies by company type, a seventeen-term model term sheet, a phased implementation roadmap, a risk register and a review of related literature. Published in a personal capacity. Not legal or financial advice.

title: Little Elpier : Higher-Order Logic, Types and λProlog, One Question at a Time
abstract: What eats a fly? Ask the pond. A small pond: algae, snails and flies, frogs and fish, a duck, a heron and an otter. Eleven short lines say who eats whom. Type a question, eats X fly, and a program answers: the frog, then the fish. It does not search the web or guess. It answers only from what the lines say, and it tells you when they say nothing. That is a logic program: a list of things that are true, and a way to ask what follows. This little book teaches the idea from zero, in the question-and-answer style of The Little Schemer. Each page is two columns, a short question on the left and a short answer on the right. Cover the answers with a card, try, then look. Now and then a box states a Maxim, a short rule the questions above it have earned, from "A fact says what is true. A question asks whether it follows." to "A typing rule is a clause. A type checker is a logic program, and it runs both ways." The language is λProlog, a younger and stranger relative of Prolog. It adds three things: types, so the computer turns away nonsense before it runs; predicates you pass around like numbers; and two small words, pi and =>, that let a program say "for any new thing" and "suppose this were true". Those three additions are what higher-order logic programming means. With them, a type checker for a little programming language fits in seven short clauses, and the same seven clauses infer types they were never told. That is where the book ends. What you will learn Facts and Questions. Constants, predicates, capital letters as holes, and what "no" really means. Rules and Recursion. :- as "if", recursion that knows when to stop, and the search tree behind every answer. Terms and Unification. Numbers built as trees, and how the engine makes two terms the same, or fails. Lists. One append, run three ways: join, check and split. A relation has no inputs and outputs until you ask it something. Types. Kinds, types and modes, and a checker that reads the program before it runs. Predicates as Values. One rule for "above", "upstream of" and "older than"; map, filter and fold. Lambdas. Predicates without names, terms with holes, and binders that cannot be captured. Pi and Implication. What-if questions about a pond that is not quite this one. The Little Type Checker. Seven clauses that check the types of a little language and, asked with a hole, infer them. Who it is for Students and programmers who have never taken a logic course. You need some programming in any language, a pencil, and patience. No mathematics, no Prolog and no Lean are assumed. You do not need to know what ∀ means; by Chapter 8 you will have written it. A chapter is an evening's work. What you get 9 short chapters, 541 questions with their answers, and 11 Maxims collected on one page 35 exercises graded ★ to ★★★, each with a solution that runs 14 diagrams: the food web, search trees, term trees, and binders A two-page cheat sheet and a guided "Where to Go Next" The Apache-2.0 companion code at github.com/Volland/little-elpier: every program in the book, with every printed output kept as a golden file that a test checks Every example runs The engine is lean-elpi, an implementation of the ELPI dialect of λProlog written in Lean 4. pip install leanelpi gives you the whole engine with nothing to compile, on macOS, Linux and Windows with WSL; a Docker image and a build from source work too. The book's site, volland.github.io/little-elpier, has a sample of the frames.
